body:
Natural hazards become disasters through their effects on people

Earthquakes, tsunamis and tropical cyclones are natural phenomena. They become disasters when they cause serious losses and disrupt the normal functioning of a community. The size of a natural event matters, but the damage it causes also depends on where people live, how buildings are constructed and how prepared the community is.

Disaster risk depends on the interaction of a hazard with exposed people and assets, their vulnerability and their capacity to withstand and recover from its effects.

Hazard means a potentially damaging event or process. Exposure means the presence of people, buildings, roads, farms or other assets in places where the hazard may occur. Vulnerability means the conditions that make those exposed elements more likely to suffer damage. Capacity includes the resources, knowledge, infrastructure and institutions that help reduce losses.

For example, 2 buildings may experience similar earthquake shaking but suffer different damage because one has stronger structural connections. Similarly, 2 coastal villages exposed to the same cyclone may experience different losses because one has safer shelters, reliable warning communication and a practiced evacuation plan.

Different physical causes require different safety measures

HazardPhysical causeMain dangerWarning characteristic
EarthquakeSudden release of energy, usually along a geological faultGround shaking, building failure and secondary hazardsExact occurrence cannot presently be predicted reliably
TsunamiSudden displacement of a large volume of seawaterRapid coastal flooding, powerful currents and debrisWarnings may follow detection of the triggering event
Tropical cycloneOrganised rotating low-pressure system sustained by warm, moist oceanic airStrong winds, storm surge and heavy rainfallTrack and intensity can often be forecast before landfall

An earthquake is a geological hazard. A tsunami is a water-wave hazard commonly generated by a geological event. A cyclone is an atmospheric hazard. Although tsunamis and storm surges both flood coasts with seawater, they have different causes and warning systems.

Four stages of managing disaster risk

  • Mitigation: Reduce potential damage before the event. Examples include earthquake-resistant buildings and avoiding unsafe coastal development.
  • Preparedness: Establish warning communication, evacuation routes, household plans and public awareness.
  • Response: Protect life and meet urgent needs during and immediately after the event through evacuation, rescue, shelter and essential relief.
  • Recovery: Restore homes, services, infrastructure and livelihoods while reducing vulnerability to future disasters.

These stages are connected. A community that reconstructs damaged houses without improving their safety may remain vulnerable to the next event. Building back better means using recovery and reconstruction to improve safety and resilience rather than merely restoring the earlier level of risk.

Prelims focus

  • Hazard and disaster are not interchangeable terms.
  • Exposure identifies what is located in a hazard-prone area; vulnerability identifies why it is susceptible to damage.
  • Earthquake occurrence cannot presently be predicted reliably at an exact place and time.
  • Tsunami warnings and cyclone forecasts are based on different physical monitoring systems.
  • Trap: Storm surge is not another name for tsunami.

[Sources: National Disaster Management Authority, National Disaster Management Plan, 2019, sections on disaster risk reduction and preparedness; National Disaster Management Authority, Guidelines for Management of Earthquakes, 2007; National Disaster Management Authority, Guidelines for Management of Tsunamis, August 2010, Chapters 1 and 5; India Meteorological Department, Cyclone Warning in India: Standard Operation Procedure, March 2021, Chapters 1 and 6. Official documents consulted 2 November 2026.]

title: Understanding Disaster Risk: Earthquakes, Tsunamis and Cyclones

body:
Why the ground shakes

An earthquake is the shaking of the ground caused by a sudden release of energy within the Earth. Most earthquakes result from movements along fractures called faults. Earth's outer rigid shell is divided into tectonic plates. Their slow relative movement can cause stress to accumulate in rocks. When the stress exceeds the resistance of the rocks, they may suddenly slip along a fault and release energy as seismic waves.

Earthquakes commonly occur near plate boundaries, but they can also occur within plates on existing faults. Consequently, areas away from major plate boundaries cannot automatically be considered free from earthquake risk.

Focus and epicentre

The focus, also called the hypocentre, is the location inside the Earth where earthquake rupture begins. The epicentre is the point on the Earth's surface directly above the focus. Seismic waves travel outward from the earthquake source and produce ground motion over an area.

The strongest damage is often concentrated near the source, but it does not always occur exactly at the epicentre. Fault-rupture characteristics, distance, soil conditions and building vulnerability also affect the distribution of damage.

Magnitude and intensity measure different things

ConceptWhat it describesImportant distinction
MagnitudeOverall size of an earthquakeNormally expressed as a single value for the event
IntensitySeverity of shaking and observed effects at a particular locationCan differ from place to place during the same earthquake
SeismographInstrument that records ground motionProvides observations used in earthquake analysis

The Richter scale is a familiar historical magnitude scale. Modern scientific reports commonly use moment magnitude, written as Mw, particularly for larger earthquakes. Magnitude scales are logarithmic rather than ordinary linear scales. A higher magnitude signifies a substantially larger earthquake, but magnitude alone cannot predict the damage at a particular settlement.

Intensity may be described using the Modified Mercalli Intensity scale, which relates shaking to experienced and observed effects. An earthquake can therefore have one reported magnitude but different intensity levels across affected locations.

India's seismic zones

Seismic zonation identifies regions with differing levels of expected earthquake shaking hazard for planning and structural design. Under the applicable Indian seismic zoning map based on IS 1893 (Part 1):2016, India is divided into 4 zones:

ZoneRelative seismic hazard
Zone IILowest of the 4 mapped categories
Zone IIIModerate
Zone IVHigh
Zone VHighest of the 4 mapped categories

Applicable standard at the content cutoff

As of 2 November 2026, the Ministry of Earth Sciences confirms that the seismic zoning map under IS 1893 (Part 1):2016 remains the applicable standard. A revised zonation associated with the 2025 standard was withdrawn in March 2026. Therefore, the applicable zonation discussed here contains Zones II, III, IV and V; a proposed additional zone should not be treated as operative.

Parts of the Himalayan region, northeastern India and the Rann of Kutch are associated with high earthquake hazard. Gujarat does not have one uniform level of seismic hazard across its entire territory. A zone classification indicates regional hazard; it does not establish whether an individual building is safe or unsafe.

What can and cannot be predicted

Scientists can identify active faults, monitor seismicity, estimate long-term regional hazard and record earthquake locations after events occur. However, a scientifically reliable method for predicting the precise place, time and magnitude of a future earthquake is not available. Earthquake early-warning systems, where implemented, detect an earthquake after rupture begins and may provide a short warning before strong shaking reaches some locations. They do not predict the earthquake before it starts.

Prelims focus

  • Focus or hypocentre: underground point where earthquake rupture begins.
  • Epicentre: surface point directly above the focus.
  • Magnitude measures earthquake size; intensity describes local effects.
  • Applicable Indian seismic zones: II, III, IV and V.
  • Zone V represents the highest seismic hazard category.
  • Trap: Seismic monitoring and early warning are not the same as predicting a future earthquake.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Environment, Class 7, Chapter 3, Our Changing Earth, printed pp. 12–14, 2018–19 printing; NCERT, Science, Class 8, Chapter 15, Some Natural Phenomena, printed pp. 191–194, 2018–19 printing; Bureau of Indian Standards and National Disaster Management Authority, Simplified Guidelines for Earthquake Safety of Buildings, based on National Building Code of India 2016, Section 2.1; Ministry of Earth Sciences, Parliament Question: Seismograph Network, 1 April 2026, statement on IS 1893 and withdrawal of revised zonation. Official sources consulted 2 November 2026.]

title: Earthquake Causes, Measurement and Seismic Zones in India

body:
Why some buildings suffer more damage

Ground shaking does not affect every structure in the same way. A building's performance depends on the shaking it experiences, the characteristics of its supporting ground and the way the building was planned, built and maintained. Earthquake-resistant construction aims to reduce the likelihood of serious structural failure and loss of life.

Several conditions can increase vulnerability:

  • Unreinforced masonry: Brick or stone walls without adequate reinforcing and connections may crack or separate during lateral shaking.
  • Weak connections: Poor connections between walls, floors and roofs can allow parts of a building to move or fail separately.
  • Open or soft ground storey: A relatively weak or flexible lower floor, such as one with extensive open parking, can concentrate deformation and suffer severe damage.
  • Structural irregularity: Abrupt changes in building shape, height, mass or stiffness can lead to uneven earthquake response.
  • Heavy or unsecured components: Falling parapets, ceilings, water tanks, shelves and other objects may injure people even where the main structure remains standing.

Height alone does not determine safety. A properly designed and constructed taller building may perform better than a poorly built shorter structure. Similarly, a newer building is not necessarily safe merely because it is new. Quality of design, materials, connections and construction remains important.

Liquefaction: when shaken soil loses strength

Soil liquefaction is a condition in which certain water-saturated, usually loose granular soils lose much of their strength and stiffness during strong shaking because pore-water pressure increases.

Under ordinary conditions, soil grains support loads through contact with one another. During sufficiently strong shaking, a susceptible saturated soil may develop increased pressure in the water occupying spaces between its grains. The effective contact forces between grains decrease, and the soil may temporarily behave in a fluid-like manner.

Possible effects include uneven settlement, tilting of buildings, ground cracking, lateral movement of soil and damage to buried utilities. Low-lying land, reclaimed ground and some river or coastal deposits may contain susceptible soils, but liquefaction does not occur in every wet soil or during every earthquake. Soil type, density, saturation and shaking conditions matter.

Indian standards for earthquake safety

The Bureau of Indian Standards publishes technical standards used by qualified professionals for seismic design, construction and assessment. Their central purposes should be distinguished in objective questions.

StandardPrincipal purpose
IS 1893 (Part 1):2016Criteria for earthquake-resistant design and the applicable seismic zoning basis
IS 4326:2013Earthquake-resistant design and construction of buildings
IS 13920:2016Ductile design and detailing of reinforced-concrete structures subjected to seismic forces
IS 15988:2013Seismic evaluation and strengthening of existing reinforced-concrete buildings
IS 13935:2009Seismic evaluation, repair and strengthening of masonry buildings

Ductility is the ability of a structural component to deform significantly while retaining useful strength and avoiding sudden brittle failure. In earthquakes, this characteristic is valuable because structures must accommodate movement rather than simply resist an unmoving load.

Retrofitting existing buildings

Seismic retrofitting means improving an existing building's earthquake performance through appropriate strengthening or modification. Depending on professional assessment, this can involve improving the connections between structural elements, strengthening vulnerable components or correcting major weaknesses in the load-resisting system.

Retrofitting differs from ordinary maintenance. Painting cracks or repairing surface plaster may restore appearance but does not necessarily address underlying structural vulnerability. Retrofitting also differs from constructing a completely new building to current earthquake-resistant requirements.

Earthquake-resistant does not mean earthquake-proof. Appropriate design, construction and retrofitting reduce the risk of severe damage or collapse, but no building should be assumed immune to all possible shaking.

Public authorities can reduce earthquake losses by encouraging compliance with applicable building requirements, assessing the safety of schools and hospitals, discouraging unsafe construction and improving public awareness. Structural evaluation and design decisions require suitably qualified professionals.

Prelims focus

  • Liquefaction is associated with susceptible, water-saturated soils during strong shaking.
  • An open or weak ground storey can make a building vulnerable.
  • IS 1893 concerns earthquake-resistant design criteria.
  • IS 13920 concerns ductile detailing of reinforced-concrete structures.
  • IS 15988 concerns evaluation and strengthening of existing reinforced-concrete buildings.
  • Trap: Retrofitting is structural risk reduction, not merely cosmetic repair.

[Sources: Bureau of Indian Standards and National Disaster Management Authority, Simplified Guidelines for Earthquake Safety of Buildings, based on National Building Code of India 2016, Sections 2.1–2.2 and discussion of building vulnerability; Bureau of Indian Standards, standards records for IS 1893 (Part 1):2016, IS 4326:2013, IS 13920:2016 and IS 15988:2013; NCERT, Science, Class 8, Chapter 15, Some Natural Phenomena, printed pp. 194–195, 2018–19 printing. Official sources consulted 2 November 2026.]
